title: Luke, looking back
hookLine: outsiders, women, the poor, the lost found
tomorrow: John's Gospel has no manger. so where does it begin?

cards: A night shift is a lonely shift: the security desk, the hospital floor, the last delivery van. In Luke, the first big announcement goes to the night shift.
Shepherds in a field near Bethlehem, nobody's idea of honored guests, and an angel says: “Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.”
Great joy, for everyone, delivered first to the ones awake at work. And Luke's last lines have the same two words: the disciples go back to Jerusalem “with great joy.”

teach.b: Between those two joys, Luke keeps setting a bigger table: women named among those who traveled with Jesus and provided for the group, a rich tax collector up a tree, a chapter of lost things, a sheep, a coin, a son, each ending in a party.
Then Luke's blessing: “Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.” Here Christians have a real debate.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: THE POOR MEANS THE POOR.
teach.b: One side says Luke means the poor, people with little money. The same sermon says, “woe unto you that are rich!”
Jesus opens his work by reading good news to the poor, and Luke's parties keep happening at the bottom of the ladder. Read plainly, it asks something of anyone with a full barn.

teach.h: OTHER SIDE: ANYONE WHO IS LOST.
teach.b: The other side says Matthew's version reads “poor in spirit,” and Luke's own rich man, Zacchaeus, is found too: “For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
So the poor are anyone who knows they can't save themselves, rich or not. Each side keeps something the other needs.
One won't let the words float away from real hunger. The other won't let anyone be shut out by a bank balance.
And in Acts, written to the same Theophilus, Paul tells a crowd that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men.”

how: Christians hear Luke's shepherds and the good tidings of great joy read at Christmas, and some churches put Luke's welcome into practice with shared meals and hospitality for newcomers.

s: the wise men are in Luke's Christmas story
they're in Matthew. Luke's first visitors are shepherds on the night shift.
Luke's blessing says 'blessed be ye poor', without 'in spirit'
Matthew has 'poor in spirit'. Christians read the two together in different ways.
in Luke, 'great joy' belongs only to Christmas
it's in the book's last lines too: they returned to Jerusalem with great joy.

games.q: your friend reads 'blessed be ye poor' and says it's only about money; the spiritual reading lets rich people off the hook. what's the best case for the other side?
o: Matthew says 'poor in spirit', so Luke's version is simply a mistake.
Zacchaeus is rich and still found: the poor can mean anyone who knows they're lost.
the Bible never really talks about money, so it has to be spiritual.
games.why: a good steelman uses the other side's own best evidence. Luke's rich tax collector is sought and saved; the money reading keeps 'woe unto you that are rich'. both stay on the table.

practice: Bring to mind one person at the edge of a room you're often in: the new kid, the coworker who eats alone, the cousin who sits apart.
If it's a good moment, send them one short message that asks for nothing back; if not, decide where you'll save them a seat. If you pray, hold their name through the sit.

wordCard.voice: Luke. The Gospel that starts its great joy with shepherds on the night shift and keeps finding the people at the edge.

orig.note: Greek: great joy, from Luke 2:10. Luke 24:52 says it again, in the book's last lines.

carryVoice: Keep this one: great joy, which in Luke breaks out wherever the lost are found. See you tomorrow.
